In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the early immunologic response to transplantation, the role of cytokines in the development of acute rejection, and the prognostic relevance of cytokine levels.
the role of cytokines as markers of rejection or infection in kidney transplantation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IL-6, and IL-8, are useful as early indicators of the course of transplant rejection, and IL-6 is a useful indicator of septic complications.
IL-6, and especially IL-6 in urine, are the most sensitive and specific markers of acute rejection.
the IL-6, the IL-8, or the IL-10 level in blood or urine does not provide any additional prognostic information to the clinical parameters of renal transplantation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the early posttransplantation IL-6,IL-8, andIL-10 serum levels in the first 24 hours after transplantation are predictive of rejection, sepsis, and transplant dysfunction in the following weeks.

we have shown that the measurement of IL-6 levels in the serum of patients with acute rejection is a reliable marker of the presence of acute rejection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the early postoperative IL-6, and IL-8, IL-10 levels are not good markers of the evolution after kidney transplantation.
IL-6, in addition to being an early marker of acute rejection, also may predict the risk of septic complications.
IL-6 and IL-8 may be used as early markers for the detection of rejection and sepsis.
